grammar_points.name: 〜だって (datte: even if)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add だって (datte) or って (tte) after the past tense of a verb to express 'even if'. After nouns, だって means 'even [noun]'.

Example from this song: 転んだって (korondatte) = 'even if you fall down' — from 転ぶ (korobu, 'to fall') → 転んだ (koronda, past) + って (tte, 'even if')

More examples:
• 失敗する (shippai suru, 'to fail') → 失敗したって (shippai shitatte, 'even if you fail')
• 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣いたって (naitatte, 'even if you cry')
• 何 (nani, 'what') → 何だって (nan datte, 'anything/no matter what')

Note: たって is the casual version of ても (temo). Both mean 'even if': 転んでも = 転んだって. たって/だって is more colloquial and common in hip-hop lyrics like this song.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 転ぶ (korobu, 'to fall') → 転んだ (koronda, past) + って (tte, 'even if') → 転んだって (korondatte, 'even if you fall')

grammar_points.name: 〜ぜ (ze: masculine emphasis)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add ぜ (ze) at the end of a sentence for strong masculine assertion. It conveys confidence, excitement, and determination. Very common in hip-hop and shonen anime.

Example from this song: いいぜ (ii ze) = 'It's good!' / 行くぜ (iku ze) = 'Let's go!' — ぜ turns statements into confident declarations.

More examples:
• やる (yaru, 'to do') → やるぜ (yaru ze, 'I'll do it, yeah!')
• 負けない (makenai, 'won't lose') → 負けないぜ (makenai ze, 'I won't lose!')
• 最高 (saikou, 'the best') → 最高だぜ (saikou da ze, 'It's the best!')

Note: ぜ is strongly masculine and casual. Using it in formal settings would be inappropriate. In this hip-hop track, it perfectly matches the high-energy, confident tone. Strength ranking: ぞ (strongest) > ぜ > よ (mildest).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: いい (ii, 'good') + ぜ (ze, emphasis) → いいぜ (ii ze, 'It's good!') / 行く (iku, 'to go') + ぜ (ze) → 行くぜ (iku ze, 'Let's go!')

grammar_points.name: 〜となる (to naru: to become)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use noun + と (to) + なる (naru, 'to become') to express transformation — something becomes something else. と marks what it transforms into.

Example from this song: 勇気となる (yuuki to naru) = 'becomes courage' — from 勇気 (yuuki, 'courage') + と (to, 'into') + なる (naru, 'to become')

More examples:
• 力 (chikara, 'strength') → 力となる (chikara to naru, 'becomes strength')
• 光 (hikari, 'light') → 光となる (hikari to naru, 'becomes light')
• 問題 (mondai, 'problem') → 問題となる (mondai to naru, 'becomes a problem')

Note: となる is slightly more formal/literary than になる (ni naru). Both mean 'become', but となる often implies a more significant or dramatic transformation. In songs and literature, となる adds weight.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 勇気 (yuuki, 'courage') + と (to, 'into') + なる (naru, 'to become') → 勇気となる (yuuki to naru, 'becomes courage')

grammar_points.name: 〜でしょ (desho: right?; isn't it?)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add でしょ (desho) at the end of a statement to seek confirmation or express assumption — 'right?' or 'isn't it?'. It's the casual form of でしょう (deshou).

Example from this song: 覚悟でしょ (kakugo desho) = 'you're prepared, right?' — from 覚悟 (kakugo, 'readiness/resolve') + でしょ (desho, 'right?')

More examples:
• 分かる (wakaru, 'to understand') → 分かるでしょ (wakaru desho, 'you understand, right?')
• 寒い (samui, 'cold') → 寒いでしょ (samui desho, 'it's cold, right?')
• 本当 (hontou, 'true') → 本当でしょ (hontou desho, 'it's true, right?')

Note: With rising intonation, でしょ seeks confirmation. With falling intonation, it asserts 'I told you so'. でしょう (long form) is more polite; でしょ (short) is casual.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 覚悟 (kakugo, 'resolve') + でしょ (desho, 'right?') → 覚悟でしょ (kakugo desho, 'you're prepared, right?')

grammar_points.name: 命令形 (imperative form)

explanation.en:
How it works: Change the verb ending to create a direct command. For -ru verbs (ichidan), replace る with ろ. For -u verbs (godan), change the final syllable to its え-row equivalent.

Example from this song: 上げろ (agero) = 'Raise it!' — from 上げる (ageru, 'to raise') → replace る with ろ = 上げろ (agero)

More examples:
• 立つ (tatsu, 'to stand') → 立て (tate, 'Stand up!')
• 見る (miru, 'to look') → 見ろ (miro, 'Look!')
• 来る (kuru, 'to come') → 来い (koi, 'Come!') — irregular

Note: In this hip-hop track, the imperative carries rallying energy — 'raise your voice!' 'stand up!' Ichidan: る→ろ. Godan: final syllable → え-row. Irregulars: する→しろ (shiro), 来る→来い (koi).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 上げる (ageru, 'to raise') → 上げろ (agero, 'Raise it!')

grammar_points.name: 〜だけ (dake: only; just)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add だけ (dake) after a noun, verb, or number to restrict meaning to 'only' or 'just'. It limits the scope to exactly what's mentioned.

Example from this song: 繰り返すだけの (kurikaesu dake no) = 'just/only repeating' — from 繰り返す (kurikaesu, 'to repeat') + だけ (dake, 'only') + の (no, connecting)

More examples:
• 一つ (hitotsu, 'one') → 一つだけ (hitotsu dake, 'just one')
• 見る (miru, 'to see') → 見るだけ (miru dake, 'just looking')
• 少し (sukoshi, 'a little') → 少しだけ (sukoshi dake, 'just a little')

Note: だけ is neutral — it simply limits. Compare with しか (shika) + negative, which implies disappointment: 一つだけある (hitotsu dake aru, 'there's just one') vs. 一つしかない (hitotsu shika nai, 'there's only one [unfortunately]').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 繰り返す (kurikaesu, 'to repeat') + だけ (dake, 'only') + の (no) → 繰り返すだけの (kurikaesu dake no, 'just repeating')
